newsitem.title: UK: British trade unions welcome changes under Labour.
newsitem.headline: British trade unions welcome changes under Labour.

text.p: Positive trends in British employment rights, reflecting a "change in mood" since the arrival of the new Labour government in May, were welcomed by the main umbrella body for unions on Monday.
Outlining what will come up at its annual conference in September, the Trades Union Congress (TUC) said it had drawn up motions applauding the new government's approach to various employment issues.
"Congress welcomes the new Labour government's commitment to transform Britain into a high paid, high productivity, high skilled economy," the TUC said in its agenda statement.
In particular, the union body was encouraged by the state's decision since May to:
-- sign up to the European Union's Social Chapter, a legal framework for workers' rights
-- set up a commission to establish a minimum wage, and
-- get 250,000 under-25s off benefit pay and into work using money from a one-off tax on utilities.
The TUC also welcomed Labour's project to help the long-term unemployed gain skills to find jobs.

The four-day conference, running from September 8 to 11 at Brighton on the south coast of England, will highlight British unions' drive to act as "social partners" with employers and government, moving away from the more confrontational style seen in the 1970s and 80s.
Discussions are likely to centre on the urgent need to increase union membership in Britain, which has dropped to just a third of the total workforce from a half of all workers in 1979.
The TUC said it would urge the ruling Labour Party to withdraw anti-trade union laws introduced by the former Conservative government since 1979.
